name: The Ashanti Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Ashanti Empire: From Asantehene to Enslaved
period: 1764–1896 (from Osei Kwadwo's reforms to the exile of Prempeh I)

tiers.name: The king
tiers.you: You sit on the Golden Stool as king of all Asante, and only you may pass a sentence of death; but you may not ignore the decisions of the Asanteman council, and if you break your oaths the kingmakers can destool you.
tiers.kid: The Asantehene was the king of the Asante, and his throne was the sacred Golden Stool.
tiers.rise: The senior woman of the royal lineage nominated the eligible men, the elders chose, and the assembled people could reject the choice; between reigns the Mamponghene ruled as regent. A king who broke his oaths could be destooled, as Kusi Obodom was after a failed invasion of Dahomey.
tiers.why: The Asantehene, king of all Asante, was enthroned on the Golden Stool, the Sika dwa, believed to house the spirit of the nation: the living, the dead and those yet to be born.

tiers.name: Paramount chiefs
tiers.you: You rule one of the metropolitan states with full powers of government and justice and sit on the Asanteman council, whose decisions even the Asantehene may not ignore.
tiers.kid: Paramount chiefs ruled the Asante states under the king and met in his great council.
tiers.rise: A paramount chief was elected from the female line that provided his state’s chiefs, as the Asantehene was, and swore fealty to the one above him; like the king, he could be destooled for breaking his oaths.
tiers.why: The empire joined metropolitan states, whose people were Asante citizens, to provincial states, kingdoms it had absorbed.

tiers.name: Queen mothers
tiers.you: You are the senior woman of your chief’s line: he is your son or your sister’s son, he was installed only after you were consulted, and you settle the disputes of the women of his state.
tiers.kid: Queen mothers helped choose the chiefs and kings, and judged quarrels between women.
tiers.rise: A queen mother was a senior woman of the female line that provided the chiefs, and she kept a voice in the choice of each of them.
tiers.why: Beside the chiefs stood the queen mothers.

tiers.name: Divisional chiefs
tiers.you: You speak for your mother’s family as chief of a division of villages, advise your paramount chief and wear the silk and kente the law keeps for people of rank.
tiers.kid: Divisional chiefs ruled groups of villages and gave advice to the paramount chiefs.
tiers.rise: An ohene was chosen from the female line that provided his division’s chiefs and, like any chief, could be destooled for breaking his oaths.
tiers.why: Below the paramount chiefs stood the divisional chiefs, the highest order in each state’s divisions, which grouped many villages together.

tiers.name: Officials of Kumasi
tiers.you: The Asantehene appointed you for your skill in diplomacy; you work in the foreign office in Kumasi, which handles the kingdom’s dealings with the British, French, Dutch and Arabs.
tiers.kid: Skilled officials in Kumasi ran the king’s government, and some wrote down records.
tiers.rise: Office came by the Asantehene’s appointment and, from Osei Kwadwo’s reign, by ability rather than birth, so that even foreigners could serve.
tiers.why: The Asantehene governed through a bureaucracy in Kumasi with separate ministries, among them a foreign office, small but divided into departments for relations with the British, French, Dutch and Arabs, and in the 19th…

tiers.name: Big men
tiers.you: Your trade has made you rich and served the whole state, so you carry the elephant tail of an obirempon and sit as the supreme judge of your region.
tiers.kid: Rich traders who helped the kingdom were honoured as “big men” and given an elephant tail as a badge.
tiers.rise: The title was earned rather than inherited: trade that benefited the whole state, or deeds of valour, brought it by the state’s award.
tiers.why: Successful entrepreneurs who gathered great wealth and many followers, or who distinguished themselves by heroic deeds, were honoured as abirempon (singular obirempon), “big men”.

tiers.name: Guards, police and road wardens
tiers.you: You serve in the Kumasi police, known by your long hair, and no one passes in or out of the city without the government’s permission.
tiers.kid: Police with long hair guarded Kumasi, and road wardens checked travellers and collected tolls.
tiers.rise: These forces served the Asantehene and his government directly; the sources say little about how their men were chosen.
tiers.why: The metropolitan districts had several police forces.

tiers.name: Free Asante
tiers.term: odikro (village chief), abusua panyin (head of a lineage)
tiers.you: You farm yams and plantains with your mother’s lineage under your village chief, wear cotton, and since Osei Kwame Panyin’s law no one may sell you into slavery.
tiers.kid: Most Asante were farmers who grew yams and plantains and lived in villages led by a chief.
tiers.rise: Trade that served the state could make a commoner an obirempon, and since Osei Kwadwo’s reign the king’s offices went by ability; a capital crime could bring death, though banishment or imprisonment was the more common penalty.
tiers.why: Most people were free Asante, the amanfo, citizens of the metropolitan states, and most of them farmed.

tiers.name: Enslaved people
tiers.you: You were taken captive in war and now work on an Asante master’s farm; you may acquire wealth of your own and ask for another master if he mistreats you, but at his funeral you could be killed to follow him.
tiers.kid: Enslaved people were owned by others and made to work without pay; most were captured in wars.
tiers.rise: Capture in war and tribute made people slaves; a master who married an enslaved woman could pass part of his property and status to their children. When Britain conquered Asante it let the chiefs keep their slaves, and the ban of 1908 was enforced only from the 1920s.
tiers.why: During the Atlantic slave trade Asante was the largest slave-owning and slave-trading state in the lands of present-day Ghana.
